extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, law students, regulators, and policymakers interested in rulemaking and notice-and-comment procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and critique of notice-and-comment rulemaking, ossification, and related administrative-law doctrines, focusing on how procedural requirements, judicial review, and executive oversight affect agency behavior and regulatory stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5 U.S.C. § 553(b) notice-content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory notice content requirements under 5 U.S.C. § 553(b): the notice shall include (1) a statement of the time, place, and nature of public rule making proceedings; (2) reference to the legal authority under which the rule is proposed; and (3) either the terms or substance of the proposed rule or a description of the subjects and issues involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting notices, agencies must ensure all three elements are present so interested parties have meaningful notice of the proposed rule and its legal basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5 U.S.C. § 553(c) opportunity to comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory requirement that agencies provide an opportunity for public comment during notice-and-comment rulemaking (5 U.S.C. § 553(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement implies agencies must solicit and consider public input during the rulemaking sequence and incorporate consideration of comments into final decisionmaking and explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of studies relied on during rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies upon which an agency relies in promulgating a rule must be made available during the rulemaking in order to afford interested persons meaningful notice and an opportunity for comment (American Radio Relay League, Inc v FCC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should disclose the empirical and technical bases for rules during the comment period so commenters can evaluate and critique the underlying evidence; failing to do so can undermine notice and render comments ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to respond to significant comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are required to give reasoned responses to all significant comments in a rulemaking proceeding; 'significant comments are those which, if true, raise points relevant to the agency’s decision and which, if adopted, would require a change in an agency’s proposed rule' (City of Portland v EPA; Home Box Office, Inc v FCC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'opportunity to comment is meaningless unless the agency responds to significant points.' Agencies must identify and address substantive challenges that could alter regulatory outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and treatment of 'significant comments'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'significant comment' is one that, if true, raises points relevant to the agency's decision and would require a change in the proposed rule (City of Portland v EPA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should screen comments for materiality and ensure reasoned responses to those that plausibly demand change; failing to respond risks arbitrary-and-capricious review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical outgrowth doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that a final rule must be a logical outgrowth of the proposed rule and the issues reasonably raised during notice-and-comment (discussed in the literature, e.g., Phillip M. Kannan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should ensure that the final rule does not introduce issues or substantive changes beyond what commenters could reasonably anticipate from the notice, or else risk procedural challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard-look/arbitrary-and-capricious review increases procedural burden (ossification mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heightened standards of judicial review force agencies to undertake a 'Herculean effort of assembling the record and drafting a preamble [explaining the rule as published in the Federal Register] capable of meeting judicial requirements for written justification' (summarizing ossification scholarship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The labor and evidentiary burden created by hard-look review can slow rulemaking and contribute to 'ossification' by making agencies expend significant resources on defensibility rather than on substantive regulatory design.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA/executive cost-benefit review principle
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA is charged with ensuring that 'the benefits of rules justify the costs and that the agency has selected the approach that maximizes net benefits' (Sunstein).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies subject to centralized executive review must compile cost-benefit or regulatory impact analyses; such analytic requirements can be time-consuming and resource-intensive, diverting agency resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and resource tradeoffs of compiling regulatory analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Compiling cost-benefit (or regulatory impact) analyses can be costly and time-consuming; as agencies devote more resources to meeting White House analytic demands, they will have fewer resources to devote to their core regulatory functions (Yackee and Yackee; Sunstein).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing procedural requirements, weigh analytic thoroughness against opportunity costs and the agency's capacity to perform other important tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation between economically significant rules and ossification
rubrics_metrics.description: Ossification corresponds roughly to the White House’s category of economically significant rules; such rules often attract greater procedural and analytic demands that can slow or complicate rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers and commentators should consider how thresholds for 'economically significant' treatment affect timelines, procedural burdens, and the likelihood of prolonged review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive/presidential oversight objectives and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralized oversight (e.g., Executive Orders 12291 and 12866) was intended to promote 'political accountability, interagency coordination, rational priority setting, and cost-effective rulemaking,' but oversight mechanisms (such as OIRA) have been accused of delaying or 'thwarting regulatory activity' by sitting on rules or delaying initiation of review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of oversight should account for intended governance benefits as well as potential chilling or delay effects on agency initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal rulemaking vs. informal rulemaking and hybrid procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rulemaking—with trial-like procedures—exists but has been pushed into near desuetude; formal or hybrid procedures may impose too many procedural burdens (Nielson; Samaha); some statutes (e.g., FTC procedures, Clean Air Act amendments) require additional steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate rulemaking vehicle consistent with statutory command and the tradeoffs between participation, deliberation, and speed; be mindful that added procedures can raise costs and delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency substitution/avoidance of notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are beginning to seek out alternative, less participatory regulatory vehicles to circumvent increasingly stiff and formalized structures of the informal rulemaking process (McGarity; Connor Raso collects examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for substitution that reduces public participation or accountability; such practices may reflect agency responses to procedural costs but raise concerns about legitimacy and reviewability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal stability/credible commitments as regulatory objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and their regulatory missions benefit from the temporal stability of regulations; temporal stability (credible commitments) can help achieve long-term goals, including prompting regulated parties to invest in socially productive technologies (Masur; Levinson; Blackmon & Zeckhauser).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulewriters should weigh the value of present flexibility against the social benefits of stable, credible regulatory commitments that encourage long-term investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-forcing standards and rational connection to innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may base a standard or mandate on future technology when there exists a rational connection between the regulatory target and the presumed innovation (American Petroleum Institute v EPA; Union Electric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use technology-forcing provisions when justified by statutory purpose and a rational link to expected technological developments, recognizing both their potential to spur innovation and the risks of overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of incentives as regulatory instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory tools can include incentives (e.g., tax credits, credits for voluntary conservation actions) that aim to induce preferred behavior; incentives can be a valid non-cost consideration in setting regulatory terms (cases and agency proposals cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incentive-based measures carefully to avoid undue favoritism ('picking winners') and to ensure incentives align with statutory objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: E-rulemaking: access benefits vs. quality risks
rubrics_metrics.description: e-Rulemaking reduces the costs of viewing proposals and submitting comments (especially via central websites) but risks that quality input will be lost; malicious, irrelevant material may rise to the surface and information may not reach those who need it (Bridget C.E. Dooling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using electronic platforms, implement measures to filter, prioritize, and surface high-quality comments so that agencies receive meaningful input rather than noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between speed and beneficial delay (the 'right amount' of delay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ossification is not uniformly bad: delay—an essential ingredient of 'sticky' regulations—sometimes can be good for agencies; the key question is not simply how to speed up agency action, but what is the right amount of agency delay to achieve long-term goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy prescriptions should evaluate the functional role of delay in creating credible commitments and long-term regulatory effectiveness rather than treating delay as automatically undesirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costliness of eliminating agency mistakes (optimal abuse tradeoff)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulating agencies is costly, and it would be difficult to eliminate agency mistakes in a cost-justified manner; preventing all abuses of power may be too costly (Vermeule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design procedural protections with an eye to marginal costs and benefits; excessive proceduralism to avoid all errors can produce net harms via diverted resources and ossification.
